# A New Old Play
**A New Old Play** (Chinese: 椒麻堂会; pinyin: *Jiāomá tánghuì*) is a 2021 historical drama film written, directed, and designed by the Chinese contemporary artist and filmmaker Qiu Jiongjiong. It marks Qiu's first foray into fictional feature filmmaking, following a prolific career in experimental documentary. The film is a sprawling, epic chronicle of 20th-century China, viewed through the lens of a Sichuan opera troupe and, specifically, the life of a celebrated *chou* (clown) actor named Qiu Fu. The protagonist is based on the director's own grandfather, the renowned opera performer Qiu Fuxin, anchoring the film's vast historical sweep in personal, biographical intimacy.

Spanning over five decades, the narrative traverses the tumultuous epochs of modern Chinese history, including the Warlord Era, the Second Sino-Japanese War, the Chinese Civil War, the establishment of the People's Republic of China, the Great Leap Forward, and the Cultural Revolution. However, rather than adhering to the conventions of social realist cinema, *A New Old Play* employs a highly stylized, surrealist aesthetic. Shot entirely on a soundstage in Leshan, Sichuan, the film utilizes handcrafted sets, painted backdrops, and practical effects to create a "diorama" or "tableau vivant" visual style. This aesthetic choice reflects the film's thematic preoccupation with the interplay between life and theater, reality and artifice, suggesting that history itself is a staged performance.

The film's narrative structure is non-linear, framed by Qiu Fu's journey through the underworld (Diyu) after his death in the 1980s. As he is escorted by the guardian spirits Ox-Head and Horse-Face toward the Bridge of Helplessness to drink the Soup of Forgetfulness, Qiu Fu recounts his life story. This retrospective structure allows for a fluid movement between the ghostly, bureaucratic afterlife and the vibrant, often tragic world of the living. The film engages deeply with themes of memory, oblivion, the resilience of the artist, and the specific cultural heritage of Sichuan opera.

Premiering at the 74th Locarno Film Festival in August 2021, *A New Old Play* was awarded the Special Jury Prize, garnering widespread critical acclaim for its visual inventiveness and emotional depth. Critics have hailed it as a significant work of Chinese independent cinema, noting its "Brechtian" alienation techniques and its "Sichuan-flavored" tragicomedy. Despite its success on the international festival circuit, including awards at the Festival des 3 Continents and the Hong Kong International Film Festival, the film has faced distribution challenges within mainland China due to its sensitive historical subject matter. It has been distributed in North America by Icarus Films and in France by Hippocampe Productions.

## Plot
The narrative of *A New Old Play* is a complex tapestry that weaves together the supernatural bureaucracy of the Chinese underworld with a grounded, albeit stylized, retelling of 20th-century Chinese history. The film operates on two distinct planes of existence: the monochromatic, fog-laden realm of the afterlife in the 1980s, and the vibrant, evolving world of the living from the 1920s to the 1970s. These two strands are braided together through the recollections of the protagonist, Qiu Fu.

### Descent into the Underworld
The film commences in the immediate aftermath of Qiu Fu's death. The setting is the entrance to Fengdu, the "Ghost City" of Chinese mythology, depicted here not as a place of torment but as a mundane, misty administrative zone. Qiu Fu, portrayed as an elderly man in the afterlife sequences, is met by two "psychopomps" or guides: Ox-Head and Horse-Face. In traditional folklore, these are fearsome demons, but in Qiu Jiongjiong's interpretation, they are weary, bickering low-level bureaucrats concerned with their quotas and working conditions.

The journey through the underworld is slow and deliberate, mirroring the pacing of a traditional opera. The landscape is surreal, constructed from obvious soundstage elements—smoke machines, painted flats, and artificial lighting—emphasizing the film's theatrical conceit. As they travel toward the court of the King of Hell (Yama), they stop at a roadside inn located in the liminal space between existence and oblivion. This inn serves as a gathering place for wandering souls. Here, Qiu Fu encounters familiar faces from his past, including his former servant Crooky, who now works as an innkeeper in the netherworld. It is in this suspended state, awaiting the mandatory consumption of the Soup of Forgetfulness (Mengpo Soup) which will erase his memories before reincarnation, that Qiu Fu begins to narrate the story of his life .

### The Foundling and the New-New Troupe (1920s)
The narrative transitions to the 1920s in Sichuan province, a period defined by the instability of the Warlord Era. A young Qiu Fu (played by Chen Haoyu) is introduced living in destitution. The film depicts his early trauma: his father, also a performer, dies while on stage, a foreshadowing of Qiu Fu's own lifelong commitment to the art. His mother, impoverished and unable to care for him, abandons the boy.

The young orphan is eventually taken in by the "New-New Troupe" (*Xinxin Troupe*), a local Sichuan opera company. The troupe is a microcosm of society, led by the charismatic and imposing Pocky Liu (played by Qiu Zhimin). Pocky is a former military commander who has transitioned from the battlefield to the theater, bringing with him a martial discipline. He runs the troupe with an iron fist, utilizing corporal punishment and strict training regimens, yet he also harbors a genuine passion for the art form. Pocky serves as a protector for the artists in a lawless time, shielding them from the worst depredations of the local warlords and bandits. Under the tutelage of the troupe's masters, Qiu Fu begins his rigorous training in the *chou* (clown) role. The film details the physical and psychological demands of this specialization, which requires the actor to master acrobatics, singing, and the ability to improvise humor while wearing the characteristic white paint around the nose and eyes .

### The Theater of War (1937–1949)
As Qiu Fu matures into a young adult and a leading performer (now played by Yi Sicheng), the external world intrudes violently upon the sanctuary of the theater. The outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937–1945) brings aerial bombardments to Sichuan. The film visualizes these attacks with a deliberate lack of realism; explosions and destruction are rendered through theatrical effects, such as shaking fabrics and stylized lighting changes, highlighting the "staged" nature of the violence while not diminishing its emotional impact on the characters.

During this period, the troupe faces immense hardship. Audiences dwindle, inflation soars, and the performers struggle to find food. Despite the privation, Qiu Fu's artistry matures, and he gains renown for his wit and skill. He forms a romantic bond with Tong Huafeng (played by Guan Nan), a fellow performer in the troupe. Their marriage and attempt to build a family are depicted against the backdrop of constant insecurity.

The end of the war against Japan brings no peace, as the country immediately plunges into the Chinese Civil War (1945–1949). The New-New Troupe finds itself navigating a treacherous political landscape. Pocky Liu's background as a former military man and the troupe's occasional performances for Nationalist (Kuomintang) officers make them vulnerable as the tide turns in favor of the Communists. The anxiety of the artists is palpable; they must constantly revise their repertoire and their public allegiances to ensure their survival. The film portrays this era as a time of moral ambiguity, where the line between artist and propagandist begins to blur .

### The "New Society" and Thought Reform (1950s)
With the victory of the Communist Party and the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, the New-New Troupe undergoes a profound transformation. The chaotic, market-driven environment of the past is replaced by rigid state control. The troupe is nationalized, and the performers are designated as "literary and art workers."

The narrative moves through the political campaigns of the 1950s, specifically the "Thought Reform" movements and the Anti-Rightist Campaign. The film depicts the absurdity of these ideological purity tests. Traditional operas are dissected for "feudal" elements; ghosts, emperors, and concubines are banned or rewritten. The clowns, whose role was traditionally to mock authority and social mores, are now instructed that their humor must serve the "workers, peasants, and soldiers."

Pocky Liu becomes a primary target during these campaigns. His history as a warlord and a "capitalist" owner of the troupe leads to his denunciation as a class enemy. Qiu Fu, although from a poor background, is also scrutinized for his adherence to "old society" artistic traditions. The film presents the struggle sessions and self-criticism meetings as grotesque parodies of theater, where everyone is forced to play a role in a script written by the state. The betrayal of colleagues and the erosion of trust within the troupe are central themes of this segment .

### Famine and the Pigsty (1960s–1970s)
The narrative descends into its darkest chapter with the onset of the Great Leap Forward (1958–1962) and the subsequent Cultural Revolution (1966–1976). The film does not shy away from depicting the Great Famine that ravaged Sichuan. In scenes that blend horror with surrealism, the characters are shown catching and eating rats to survive. The artistic refinement of the opera troupe stands in stark contrast to the primal struggle for biological existence.

During the Cultural Revolution, the persecution of the artists intensifies. Qiu Fu is labeled a "monster and demon" (*niuguisheshen*). The ultimate humiliation occurs when he is forced to live in a pigsty—a literalization of his status as a social pariah. The beautiful costumes and handcrafted props of the troupe are burned or confiscated, symbolizing the destruction of culture. Yet, even in the pigsty, Qiu Fu attempts to maintain a semblance of his identity. The film suggests that his training as a clown—someone who understands the inherent absurdity of the human condition—grants him a unique form of spiritual resilience. He endures the physical abuse and psychological torture with a stoic, almost detached, observation .

### The Final Curtain (1980s)
The chronological narrative concludes in the reform era of the 1980s. Qiu Fu has been "rehabilitated" politically, but he is now a broken man, physically frail and haunting a world that is rapidly modernizing and leaving traditional opera behind. He dies in an accident, bringing the story full circle to the opening scene in the underworld.

Back in the netherworld inn, Qiu Fu finishes his tale. Surrounded by the ghosts of his past—Pocky, Crooky, and others—he shares a final toast. The mood is one of resignation and melancholic acceptance. The "New Old Play" of his life has concluded. He steps onto the Bridge of Helplessness and drinks the Soup of Forgetfulness. As he consumes the broth, the memories of fifty years of struggle, art, love, and pain dissolve. He walks into the mist of reincarnation, his individual history erased, leaving only the collective memory of the film itself .

## Cast and Characters
The casting of *A New Old Play* is a significant aspect of its artistic statement. Director Qiu Jiongjiong employs a mixture of professional actors and non-professionals, drawing heavily from his own family and close circle of friends. This choice imbues the film with an intimacy and a meta-theatrical layer, as descendants often play their ancestors or variations of people they knew .

| Actor | Character | Role Description |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Yi Sicheng** | **Qiu Fu** | The protagonist, a renowned *chou* (clown) actor in the New-New Troupe. Based on the director's grandfather, Qiu Fuxin. Yi plays the adult and elderly Qiu Fu. He captures the physicality of the clown role—the gait, the expressions, and the tragicomic aura. |
| **Chen Haoyu** | **Young Qiu Fu** | Plays Qiu Fu as a child. Chen is the director's nephew, continuing the family lineage within the cast. |
| **Guan Nan** | **Tong Huafeng** | Qiu Fu's wife and a fellow opera performer. She represents the stability of the domestic sphere amidst the chaos of the troupe's life. |
| **Qiu Zhimin** | **Pocky Liu** (Liu Ma) | The founder and manager of the New-New Troupe. A former warlord officer with a pockmarked face. The character is a complex mix of benevolence and brutality. **Significantly, Qiu Zhimin is the director's father and the son of the real Qiu Fuxin.** |
| **Gu Tao** | **Crooky** (Tuo'er) | A hunchbacked servant of the troupe who appears in the afterlife as an innkeeper. The character is "aphasic" and speaks little, serving as a silent witness. Gu Tao is a notable independent documentary filmmaker. |
| **Xue Xuchun** | **Ah Hei** / **Chicken Foot** | A dual role. Ah Hei is Qiu Fu's son. Chicken Foot is a cook at the netherworld inn. |
| **Xu Gang** | **Master Zhang** | A senior master in the troupe who trains the young apprentices. |

### Character Analysis
* **Qiu Fu:** As a *chou* actor, Qiu Fu is not a heroic protagonist in the traditional sense. The *chou* in Chinese opera is allowed to speak truth to power through humor, but is also a figure of low status. Qiu Fu's survival through the changing regimes is not due to ideological fervor but to his adaptability and his clown's ability to endure humiliation. He embodies the resilience of the ordinary Sichuanese people. 
* **Pocky Liu:** Played by the director's father, Pocky is a figure of patriarchal authority. His transition from warlord to theater manager represents the shift in power dynamics in early 20th-century China. His eventual persecution highlights the indiscriminate nature of the political purges. 
* **Crooky:** This character functions as a spiritual anchor. In the underworld, he provides the space for Qiu Fu's recollection. His physical deformity and silence contrast with the articulate, performative nature of the actors, grounding the film in a somatic reality .

## Production
### Development and Inspiration
*A New Old Play* is deeply rooted in the director's personal history. Qiu Jiongjiong was born in Leshan, Sichuan, in 1977, into a family of opera performers. His grandfather, Qiu Fuxin, was a legendary *chou* actor. Qiu grew up in the theater, absorbing its aesthetics, sounds, and stories, which later informed his work as a painter and documentary filmmaker.

The direct impetus for the film came in 2017, the 30th anniversary of Qiu Fuxin's death. Qiu's father (who plays Pocky in the film) wrote a biography of the grandfather and asked Qiu Jiongjiong to provide illustrations. During the two-month process of drawing these scenes, Qiu realized the cinematic potential of the material. He began writing the screenplay in May 2017, completing a draft of over 100,000 words by February 2018\. The project was initially titled *The Neo-New Adventures*.

Qiu stated that he wanted to explore the "clown's perspective" as the "author's perspective." He viewed the clown not just as a role but as a spirit—one of sympathy, mischief, and critical observation. The film was conceived as a "Sichuan-flavored saga," aiming to capture the unique dialect and cultural temperament of his home province .

### Set Design and Visual Aesthetic
The most striking element of *A New Old Play* is its visual style. Rejecting the location shooting common in independent Chinese cinema (often associated with the "dGritty" realism of directors like Jia Zhangke), Qiu opted for total artifice.

* **Soundstage Shooting:** The entire film was shot on a soundstage in Leshan, Sichuan. 
* **Handcrafted Sets:** The production design, led by Qiu himself, is described as "handcrafted" and "artisanal." The crew spent six months building the sets using everyday materials—wood, fabric, Styrofoam, and waste materials. This aesthetic has been compared to *arte povera* (poor art), emphasizing the materiality of the objects. 
* **Painted Backdrops:** The film extensively uses 2D painted backdrops to represent environments. These are not photorealistic but expressionist, evoking the style of traditional Chinese landscape painting and the stage flats of old opera. 
* **Miniatures:** Detailed miniatures were constructed for establishing shots, including a model village and a surreal river landscape. 
* **Practical Effects:** Visual effects were achieved practically. For example, the turbulent waters of a river were simulated by crew members shaking long pieces of white fabric, a technique borrowed directly from the Peking/Sichuan opera stage .

### Cinematography
The film was photographed by **Robbin Feng** (Feng Yuchao). The cinematography complements the set design by employing a "tableau" style.

* **Aspect Ratio:** The film is presented in a **1.77:1 (16:9)** aspect ratio. This widescreen format allows for horizontal compositions that mimic the unrolling of a traditional Chinese scroll painting. 
* **Framing:** The camera often remains static or pans slowly across a scene, observing the action from a distance that mimics the proscenium arch of a theater. This reinforces the "fourth wall" and the theatricality of the presentation. 
* **Lighting:** The lighting is deliberately theatrical, often using spotlights or unnatural colors to highlight the emotional tone of a scene rather than to simulate natural light .

### Sound and Music
* **Sichuan Dialect:** The dialogue is almost entirely in the Sichuan dialect. Qiu considers the dialect essential to the film's texture, noting its "tones of vivacity, vulgarity, voracity, and... ecstasy and melancholy." 
* **Score:** The music, composed by **Diao Lili**, is derived from the percussive patterns of Sichuan opera. Gongs, cymbals, and clappers are used not just during performance scenes but as a rhythmic underscore to the narrative, punctuating the dialogue and action. The sound design creates a bridge between the diegetic world of the characters and the meta-theatrical layer of the film .

## Themes and Analysis
### The Clown as Witness and Survivor
The central theme of the film is the archetype of the **clown** (*chou*). In Chinese opera, the clown is unique; he is the only character allowed to improvise and speak directly to the audience. He is low-class but high-wisdom. Qiu Jiongjiong uses the clown as a vehicle to navigate the trauma of the 20th century. While heroes and generals (the *sheng* and *jing* roles) fall when their ideologies collapse, the clown survives because he is flexible, self-deprecating, and grounded. Qiu Fu's survival is not heroic resistance but a form of "existential persistence." The film argues that the view from the bottom—the clown's eye view—is the most honest perspective on history .

### Memory vs. Official History
The framing device of the underworld foregrounds the tension between **individual memory** and **state-sanctioned oblivion**. The "Soup of Forgetfulness" represents the erasure of personal history required by the cycle of reincarnation, but it also serves as a metaphor for the political amnesia encouraged by the state. By recounting his life before drinking the soup, Qiu Fu performs an act of resistance. He preserves the "unofficial" history of the troupe—the petty squabbles, the moments of grace, the specific textures of life—against the grand, sweeping narratives of "Revolution" and "Liberation" that seek to flatten human experience. The film is a repository for these vanishing memories .

### Theatricality and Reality
*A New Old Play* blurs the line between **life and theater**. By shooting in a deliberately artificial style, Qiu Jiongjiong suggests that for the characters, the stage is more real than the chaotic world outside. Furthermore, the film depicts political events—struggle sessions, rallies, wars—as forms of theater, often poorly scripted and violently directed. The "Brechtian" alienation effect (Verfremdungseffekt) prevents the audience from passively consuming the tragedy, encouraging a critical engagement with the mechanisms of history. The "fake" sets reveal the "truth" of the situation more effectively than a realistic reconstruction could .

### Sichuanese Optimism
Despite the grim subject matter (war, famine, persecution), the film maintains a tone of **tragicomic optimism**. This is attributed to the Sichuanese character, described by the director as having a "harmony between sorrow and joy." The depiction of the afterlife is a prime example: it is not a terrifying hell but a bureaucratic extension of life, where friends can meet for a drink. The "Ba Ba banquets"—feasts held for both weddings and funerals—symbolize this acceptance of the cycle of life and death. The film treats death not as a tragedy but as a curtain call .

## Historical Context
### Sichuan Opera (*Chuanju*)
The film serves as a love letter to **Sichuan opera**, a major school of Chinese opera that originated in the late Ming and early Qing dynasties. Unlike the more formal Peking opera, Sichuan opera is known for its humor, lively dialogue, and distinct high-pitched singing. It features five main roles: *Sheng* (male), *Dan* (female), *Jing* (painted face), *Mo* (middle-aged male), and *Chou* (clown). The film meticulously reconstructs the training methods, backstage rituals, and performance styles of the early 20th century. It also documents the decline of the art form, from the vibrant, chaotic market-town theaters of the 1920s to the sterile, state-controlled troupes of the 1950s, and finally to its marginalization in the modern era .

### Political Movements
The film provides a critical view of several key events in modern Chinese history:

* **The New Life Movement:** Briefly alluded to in the Nationalist period attempts to "civilize" the theater. 
* **The Anti-Rightist Movement (1957–1959):** Depicted through the purging of Pocky Liu. The film highlights the arbitrary nature of the labeling of "Rightists." 
* **The Great Leap Forward (1958–1962):** Portrayed through the famine. The scene of actors eating rats is a stark representation of the desperation caused by agricultural mismanagement. 
* **The Cultural Revolution (1966–1976):** The attack on the "Four Olds" (Old Customs, Old Culture, Old Habits, and Old Ideas) directly impacted the opera, which was seen as a vessel of feudal superstition. The humiliation of Qiu Fu reflects the widespread persecution of artists and intellectuals during this decade .

## Release and Reception
### Festival Run
*A New Old Play* premiered at the **Locarno Film Festival** on August 13, 2021, in the International Competition. It was a breakout success, winning the **Special Jury Prize**. It subsequently played at major festivals worldwide:

* **Festival des 3 Continents (Nantes):** Won the Young Jury Award. 
* **Hong Kong International Film Festival (HKIFF):** Won the Firebird Award for Best Film (Young Cinema Competition). 
* **International Film Festival Rotterdam (IFFR).** 
* **New York Film Festival (NYFF).** 
* **Singapore International Film Festival.** 
* **Busan International Film Festival.**

### Critical Reception
The film has received overwhelmingly positive reviews from international critics.

* **Visuals:** *The New York Times* described it as "visually magnificent," while *The New Yorker*'s Richard Brody called it "daring and imaginative." The handcrafted aesthetic was frequently cited as a refreshing departure from digital effects. 
* **Narrative:** *Variety* (via The Film Verdict) praised it as a "uniquely refined first film" but noted its "leisurely pace" might challenge some viewers. *Cinema Scope* championed Qiu as the "brightest light" in Chinese independent cinema. 
* **Thematic Depth:** Critics lauded the film's "political courage" and its poignant exploration of memory. *Screen Daily* noted the "blatant but effective" commentary on the politically reinforced changes in the arts .

### Distribution
* **North America:** Acquired by **Icarus Films** for the dGenerate Films Collection. It received a limited theatrical release (e.g., Anthology Film Archives, Museum of the Moving Image). A Blu-ray was released by **Vinegar Syndrome** under the **Kani** label in 2023\. 
* **France:** Distributed by **Hippocampe Productions**, with a theatrical release scheduled for **April 30, 2025** (or June 2025 depending on the source) . 
* **China:** The film has not received a general theatrical release in mainland China due to censorship restrictions regarding its historical content. It circulates through private screenings and the "grey market" of cinephile file sharing.

The anxiety of the artists is palpable; they must constantly revise their repertoire and their public allegiances to ensure their survival.
The film portrays this era as a time of moral ambiguity, where the line between artist and propagandist begins to blur.
With the victory of the Communist Party and the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, the New-New Troupe undergoes a profound transformation.
The chaotic, market-driven environment of the past is replaced by rigid state control.
The troupe is nationalized, and the performers are designated as "literary and art workers."
The narrative moves through the political campaigns of the 1950s, specifically the "Thought Reform" movements and the Anti-Rightist Campaign.
The film depicts the absurdity of these ideological purity tests.
Traditional operas are dissected for "feudal" elements; ghosts, emperors, and concubines are banned or rewritten.
The clowns, whose role was traditionally to mock authority and social mores, are now instructed that their humor must serve the "workers, peasants, and soldiers."
Pocky Liu becomes a primary target during these campaigns.
Pocky Liu's history as a warlord and a "capitalist" owner of the troupe leads to his denunciation as a class enemy.
Qiu Fu, although from a poor background, is also scrutinized for his adherence to "old society" artistic traditions.
The film presents the struggle sessions and self-criticism meetings as grotesque parodies of theater, where everyone is forced to play a role in a script written by the state.
The betrayal of colleagues and the erosion of trust within the troupe are central themes of this segment.
The narrative descends into its darkest chapter with the onset of the Great Leap Forward (1958–1962) and the subsequent Cultural Revolution (1966–1976).
The film does not shy away from depicting the Great Famine that ravaged Sichuan.
In scenes that blend horror with surrealism, the characters are shown catching and eating rats to survive.
The artistic refinement of the opera troupe stands in stark contrast to the primal struggle for biological existence.
During the Cultural Revolution, the persecution of the artists intensifies.
Qiu Fu is labeled a "monster and demon" (niuguisheshen).
The ultimate humiliation occurs when Qiu Fu is forced to live in a pigsty—a literalization of his status as a social pariah.
The beautiful costumes and handcrafted props of the troupe are burned or confiscated, symbolizing the destruction of culture.
Even in the pigsty, Qiu Fu attempts to maintain a semblance of his identity.
The film suggests that Qiu Fu's training as a clown—someone who understands the inherent absurdity of the human condition—grants him a unique form of spiritual resilience.
Qiu Fu endures the physical abuse and psychological torture with a stoic, almost detached, observation.
The chronological narrative concludes in the reform era of the 1980s.
Qiu Fu has been "rehabilitated" politically, but he is now a broken man, physically frail and haunting a world that is rapidly modernizing and leaving traditional opera behind.
Qiu Fu dies in an accident, bringing the story full circle to the opening scene in the underworld.
Back in the netherworld inn, Qiu Fu finishes his tale.
Surrounded by the ghosts of his past—Pocky, Crooky, and others—Qiu Fu shares a final toast.
The mood is one of resignation and melancholic acceptance.
The "New Old Play" of Qiu Fu's life has concluded.
Qiu Fu steps onto the Bridge of Helplessness and drinks the Soup of Forgetfulness.
As Qiu Fu consumes the broth, the memories of fifty years of struggle, art, love, and pain dissolve.
Qiu Fu walks into the mist of reincarnation, his individual history erased, leaving only the collective memory of the film itself.
The casting of A New Old Play is a significant aspect of its artistic statement.
Director Qiu Jiongjiong employs a mixture of professional actors and non-professionals, drawing heavily from his own family and close circle of friends.
This choice imbues the film with an intimacy and a meta-theatrical layer, as descendants often play their ancestors or variations of people they knew.
Yi Sicheng plays Qiu Fu, the protagonist and a renowned chou (clown) actor in the New-New Troupe.
The character Qiu Fu is based on the director's grandfather, Qiu Fuxin.
Yi Sicheng plays the adult and elderly Qiu Fu.
Yi Sicheng captures the physicality of the clown role—the gait, the expressions, and the tragicomic aura.
Chen Haoyu plays Qiu Fu as a child.
Chen Haoyu is the director's nephew, continuing the family lineage within the cast.
Guan Nan plays Tong Huafeng, Qiu Fu's wife and a fellow opera performer.
Tong Huafeng represents the stability of the domestic sphere amidst the chaos of the troupe's life.
Qiu Zhimin plays Pocky Liu (Liu Ma), the founder and manager of the New-New Troupe.
Pocky Liu is a former warlord officer with a pockmarked face.
The character Pocky Liu is a complex mix of benevolence and brutality.
Qiu Zhimin is the director's father and the son of the real Qiu Fuxin.
Gu Tao plays Crooky (Tuo'er), a hunchbacked servant of the troupe who appears in the afterlife as an innkeeper.
The character Crooky is "aphasic" and speaks little, serving as a silent witness.
Gu Tao is a notable independent documentary filmmaker.
Xue Xuchun plays a dual role as Ah Hei and Chicken Foot.
Ah Hei is Qiu Fu's son.
Chicken Foot is a cook at the netherworld inn.
Xu Gang plays Master Zhang, a senior master in the troupe who trains the young apprentices.
As a chou actor, Qiu Fu is not a heroic protagonist in the traditional sense.
The chou in Chinese opera is allowed to speak truth to power through humor, but is also a figure of low status.
Qiu Fu's survival through the changing regimes is not due to ideological fervor but to his adaptability and his clown's ability to endure humiliation.
Qiu Fu embodies the resilience of the ordinary Sichuanese people.
Pocky Liu, played by the director's father, is a figure of patriarchal authority.
Pocky Liu's transition from warlord to theater manager represents the shift in power dynamics in early 20th-century China.
Pocky Liu's eventual persecution highlights the indiscriminate nature of the political purges.
The character Crooky functions as a spiritual anchor.
In the underworld, Crooky provides the space for Qiu Fu's recollection.
Crooky's physical deformity and silence contrast with the articulate, performative nature of the actors, grounding the film in a somatic reality.
A New Old Play is deeply rooted in the director's personal history.
Qiu Jiongjiong was born in Leshan, Sichuan, in 1977, into a family of opera performers.
Qiu Jiongjiong's grandfather, Qiu Fuxin, was a legendary chou actor.
Qiu Jiongjiong grew up in the theater, absorbing its aesthetics, sounds, and stories, which later informed his work as a painter and documentary filmmaker.
The direct impetus for the film came in 2017, the 30th anniversary of Qiu Fuxin's death.
Qiu Jiongjiong's father (who plays Pocky in the film) wrote a biography of the grandfather and asked Qiu Jiongjiong to provide illustrations.
During the two-month process of drawing these scenes, Qiu Jiongjiong realized the cinematic potential of the material.
Qiu Jiongjiong began writing the screenplay in May 2017, completing a draft of over 100,000 words by February 2018.
The project was initially titled The Neo-New Adventures.
Qiu Jiongjiong stated that he wanted to explore the "clown's perspective" as the "author's perspective."
Qiu Jiongjiong viewed the clown not just as a role but as a spirit—one of sympathy, mischief, and critical observation.
The film was conceived as a "Sichuan-flavored saga," aiming to capture the unique dialect and cultural temperament of his home province.
The most striking element of A New Old Play is its visual style.
Rejecting the location shooting common in independent Chinese cinema (often associated with the "dGritty" realism of directors like Jia Zhangke), Qiu Jiongjiong opted for total artifice.
The entire film A New Old Play was shot on a soundstage in Leshan, Sichuan.
The production design, led by Qiu Jiongjiong himself, is described as "handcrafted" and "artisanal."
The crew spent six months building the sets using everyday materials—wood, fabric, Styrofoam, and waste materials.
This aesthetic has been compared to arte povera (poor art), emphasizing the materiality of the objects.
The film extensively uses 2D painted backdrops to represent environments.
These backdrops are not photorealistic but expressionist, evoking the style of traditional Chinese landscape painting and the stage flats of old opera.
Detailed miniatures were constructed for establishing shots, including a model village and a surreal river landscape.
Visual effects were achieved practically.
For example, the turbulent waters of a river were simulated by crew members shaking long pieces of white fabric, a technique borrowed directly from the Peking/Sichuan opera stage.
The film was photographed by Robbin Feng (Feng Yuchao).
The cinematography complements the set design by employing a "tableau" style.
The film is presented in a 1.77:1 (16:9) aspect ratio.
This widescreen format allows for horizontal compositions that mimic the unrolling of a traditional Chinese scroll painting.
The camera often remains static or pans slowly across a scene, observing the action from a distance that mimics the proscenium arch of a theater.
This reinforces the "fourth wall" and the theatricality of the presentation.
The lighting is deliberately theatrical, often using spotlights or unnatural colors to highlight the emotional tone of a scene rather than to simulate natural light.
The dialogue is almost entirely in the Sichuan dialect.
Qiu Jiongjiong considers the Sichuan dialect essential to the film's texture, noting its "tones of vivacity, vulgarity, voracity, and... ecstasy and melancholy."
The music, composed by Diao Lili, is derived from the percussive patterns of Sichuan opera.
Gongs, cymbals, and clappers are used not just during performance scenes but as a rhythmic underscore to the narrative, punctuating the dialogue and action.
The sound design creates a bridge between the diegetic world of the characters and the meta-theatrical layer of the film.
The central theme of the film is the archetype of the clown (chou).
In Chinese opera, the clown is unique; he is the only character allowed to improvise and speak directly to the audience.
The clown is low-class but high-wisdom.
Qiu Jiongjiong uses the clown as a vehicle to navigate the trauma of the 20th century.
While heroes and generals (the sheng and jing roles) fall when their ideologies collapse, the clown survives because he is flexible, self-deprecating, and grounded.
Qiu Fu's survival is not heroic resistance but a form of "existential persistence."
The film argues that the view from the bottom—the clown's eye view—is the most honest perspective on history.
The framing device of the underworld foregrounds the tension between individual memory and state-sanctioned oblivion.
The "Soup of Forgetfulness" represents the erasure of personal history required by the cycle of reincarnation, but it also serves as a metaphor for the political amnesia encouraged by the state.
By recounting his life before drinking the soup, Qiu Fu performs an act of resistance.

Qiu Fu preserves the "unofficial" history of the troupe—the petty squabbles, the moments of grace, the specific textures of life—against the grand, sweeping narratives of "Revolution" and "Liberation" that seek to flatten human experience.
The film is a repository for these vanishing memories.
A New Old Play blurs the line between life and theater.
By shooting in a deliberately artificial style, Qiu Jiongjiong suggests that for the characters, the stage is more real than the chaotic world outside.
Furthermore, the film depicts political events—struggle sessions, rallies, wars—as forms of theater, often poorly scripted and violently directed.
The "Brechtian" alienation effect (Verfremdungseffekt) prevents the audience from passively consuming the tragedy, encouraging a critical engagement with the mechanisms of history.
The "fake" sets reveal the "truth" of the situation more effectively than a realistic reconstruction could.
Despite the grim subject matter (war, famine, persecution), the film maintains a tone of tragicomic optimism.
This is attributed to the Sichuanese character, described by the director as having a "harmony between sorrow and joy."
The depiction of the afterlife is a prime example: it is not a terrifying hell but a bureaucratic extension of life, where friends can meet for a drink.
The "Ba Ba banquets"—feasts held for both weddings and funerals—symbolize this acceptance of the cycle of life and death.
The film treats death not as a tragedy but as a curtain call.
The film serves as a love letter to Sichuan opera, a major school of Chinese opera that originated in the late Ming and early Qing dynasties.
Unlike the more formal Peking opera, Sichuan opera is known for its humor, lively dialogue, and distinct high-pitched singing.
Sichuan opera features five main roles: Sheng (male), Dan (female), Jing (painted face), Mo (middle-aged male), and Chou (clown).
The film meticulously reconstructs the training methods, backstage rituals, and performance styles of the early 20th century.

The film also documents the decline of the art form, from the vibrant, chaotic market-town theaters of the 1920s to the sterile, state-controlled troupes of the 1950s, and finally to its marginalization in the modern era.
The film provides a critical view of several key events in modern Chinese history.
The New Life Movement is briefly alluded to in the Nationalist period attempts to "civilize" the theater.
The Anti-Rightist Movement (1957–1959) is depicted through the purging of Pocky Liu.
The film highlights the arbitrary nature of the labeling of "Rightists."
The Great Leap Forward (1958–1962) is portrayed through the famine.
The scene of actors eating rats is a stark representation of the desperation caused by agricultural mismanagement.

The Cultural Revolution (1966–1976) directly impacted the opera, which was seen as a vessel of feudal superstition, through the attack on the "Four Olds" (Old Customs, Old Culture, Old Habits, and Old Ideas).
The humiliation of Qiu Fu reflects the widespread persecution of artists and intellectuals during this decade.
A New Old Play premiered at the Locarno Film Festival on August 13, 2021, in the International Competition.
A New Old Play was a breakout success, winning the Special Jury Prize.
A New Old Play subsequently played at major festivals worldwide.
A New Old Play won the Young Jury Award at the Festival des 3 Continents (Nantes).
A New Old Play won the Firebird Award for Best Film (Young Cinema Competition) at the Hong Kong International Film Festival (HKIFF).
A New Old Play played at the International Film Festival Rotterdam (IFFR).
A New Old Play played at the New York Film Festival (NYFF).
A New Old Play played at the Singapore International Film Festival.
A New Old Play played at the Busan International Film Festival.
The film A New Old Play has received overwhelmingly positive reviews from international critics.
The New York Times described A New Old Play as "visually magnificent."
The New Yorker's Richard Brody called A New Old Play "daring and imaginative."
The handcrafted aesthetic of A New Old Play was frequently cited as a refreshing departure from digital effects.
Variety (via The Film Verdict) praised A New Old Play as a "uniquely refined first film" but noted its "leisurely pace" might challenge some viewers.
Cinema Scope championed Qiu Jiongjiong as the "brightest light" in Chinese independent cinema.
Critics lauded the film's "political courage" and its poignant exploration of memory.
Screen Daily noted the "blatant but effective" commentary on the politically reinforced changes in the arts.
A New Old Play was acquired by Icarus Films for the dGenerate Films Collection.
A New Old Play received a limited theatrical release (e.g., Anthology Film Archives, Museum of the Moving Image).
A Blu-ray of A New Old Play was released by Vinegar Syndrome under the Kani label in 2023.
A New Old Play is distributed in France by Hippocampe Productions.
A New Old Play has a theatrical release scheduled for April 30, 2025 (or June 2025 depending on the source) in France.
The film A New Old Play has not received a general theatrical release in mainland China due to censorship restrictions regarding its historical content.
A New Old Play circulates through private screenings and the "grey market" of cinephile file sharing in mainland China.
The original title of the film is 椒麻堂会 (Jiāomá tánghuì).
The English title of the film is A New Old Play.
The runtime of A New Old Play is 179 minutes (2 hours 59 minutes).
The aspect ratio of A New Old Play is 1.77:1 (16:9).
A New Old Play uses Color / Black & White (Stylized).
The audio of A New Old Play is in Sichuanese Dialect (DTS-HD MA 5.1).
A New Old Play is a film from Hong Kong and France.
The production companies for A New Old Play are Uluka Productions (HK), Hippocampe Productions (France), and Midnight Blur (China).
The sales agent for A New Old Play is Parallax Films.

4.title: A New Old Play
4.description: True to its title, Qiu Jiongjiong’s A New Old Play (2021) operates as a series of contrasts. For his narrative feature debut, the artist and documentarian has crafted a film that simultaneously serves as a detailed account of China’s turbulent political history throughout the 20th century, and a deeply personal work that incorporates elements of his own family’s history. It’s an exploration of traditional Chinese opera forms as much as it is an exercise in Brechtian alienation.
4.content:
True to its title, Qiu Jiongjiong’s _A New Old Play_ (2021) operates as a series of contrasts. For his narrative feature debut, the artist and documentarian has crafted a film that simultaneously serves as a detailed account of China’s turbulent political history throughout the 20th century, and a deeply personal work that incorporates elements of his own family’s history. It’s an exploration of traditional Chinese opera forms as much as it is an exercise in Brechtian alienation. It’s a thesis on Chinese thanatology and a satire of the mythology surrounding death and the afterlife that informs our everyday lives.

The film follows the spirit of Qiu Fu, the newly deceased leader of a Sichuan-based opera troupe, as he revisits events from his past life prior to consuming _mihuntang_, the “soup of forgetfulness” that causes souls to shed all memories and knowledge of their past life. Qiu Fu is accompanied in Diyu—the Taoist concept of the underworld that one must pass through before reincarnation—by Ox-Head and Horse-Face, two guardians of the underworld tasked with retrieving the souls of the dead, yet who spend most of their time drinking, reminiscing, and lamenting their working conditions to their ward.

Each memory Qiu Fu revisits plays out against a constantly changing political backdrop, beginning with his joining the troupe at the age of seven during republican China’s nascent years of the 1920s, and concluding with his final years in the aftermath of the Cultural Revolution of the 1960s and ‘70s. Each institution that ascends to power in his lifetime comes with different implications concerning the role and value of the theater for its own political ends. To Qiu Fu and his colleagues, a regime change may lead to continued patronage, albeit at the expense of becoming propagandists for the nationalist Kuomintang or the Chinese Communist Party, just as easily as it may lead to the scapegoating of artists and other individuals at the fringes of Chinese “political theater” for the industrial failures brought on by the economic reconstructions of the Great Leap Forward.

Qiu (the filmmaker) interweaves these multiple personal, political, and mythological layers, underscoring the ways in which each forms part of a greater societal whole. Events that take place in the political realm have ramifications in the realm of the dead, with the widespread famine of the late ‘50s & early ‘60s leading to overwork and lapses in judgment on the part of Ox-Head and Horse-Face. As time passes, political differences among Qiu Fu’s family and colleagues metastasize into personal strife. Religion itself becomes the perceived enemy of progress; the old customs practiced by some now viewed as ideologically opposed to the revolution campaigned for by others. The longer Qiu Fu lingers in this space between lives, the more these boundaries between the living and the dead, the real and artificial, old and new, become blurred, until the only constant is his theater.

Ironically, the one major figure from Chinese thanatology conspicuously missing from Qiu Fu’s experience in the underworld is Wuchang Gui, whose name translates literally to “Ghost of Impermanence.” Wuchang _Gui_ is the deity charged with escorting souls through Diyu,with the power to reward those who have committed good deeds in their lifetimes, and administer punishment to those who have committed evil. Their absence here speaks volumes, as if the filmmaker is suggesting the figure serves no function to those whose time on Earth has been marked by a state of impermanence, and whose knowledge of what actions were worthy of reward versus punishment was constantly being erased with each of the country’s political reincarnations.

In the end, Qiu Jiongjiong remains hopeful as to the country’s future. New institutions may rise where the old ones once stood, but like castles built on sand, their strength and resiliency are ultimately no match for the shifting tide. To draw from the filmmaker’s own words, enough time passes and eventually waves will bring pearls to the shore.

5.title: A NEW OLD PLAY: Director Qiu Jiongjiong Interviewed by Producer Ding Ningyuan
5.description: Director Qiu Jiongjiong Interviewed by Producer Ding Ningyuan
5.content:
![Image 1: ree](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/0e9f01_f2df203cf6064bb7b79b6513d4d29de0~mv2.jpeg/v1/fill/w_350,h_490,al_c,q_80,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/0e9f01_f2df203cf6064bb7b79b6513d4d29de0~mv2.jpeg)

English translation by John Pao-chuan Wang

_Ding Ningyuan: This film is based on your grandfather's life experience, what motivated you to make this film?_

Qiu Jiongjiong: My grandfather was a well-known Sichuan opera clown actor. He gained fame during the 1930s and performed until his death in the 1980s. I had a very close relationship with him during the first ten years of my life, and he was a crucial figure in my artistic inspirations which included painting, literature, choreography, music, and acting. It was in him that I first became fascinated with humor, creativity, and formed my initial understanding of comedy: that the strength of humor resides in fascinating individuals.

Before this film, my main focus was in documentary filmmaking and painting. My films, which often centered on the livelihoods of those around me, were like my paintings; they required the same excruciating, detail-oriented attention as that of realistic portraiture as well as the impressionistic strokes of fabulous frenzy and contrastingly melancholic colors. Traits that all tie back to the characteristics of a clown.

In 2017, on the 30th anniversary of my grandfather's passing, my father completed a biographical account of my grandfather and asked me to provide some illustrations for the book. Two months of continuous drawing inspired my desire to tell my grandfather’s story, a clown’s story, through the medium of film. My father's biography provided some of the necessary materials, and through a vast amount of additional background research I conducted, I began to piece together the story of an ordinary man, a man who embodied the spirit of a clown, living through the greatest upheavals of our times. There is nothing new under the sun, as we know. However, these characters are just like you and me, and we each in our own way will continue to repeat this same song of humanity.

_DN: What is the meaning of the clown to you, and what do you think it represents?_

QJJ: The character of the clown is represented frequently in and is almost ubiquitous with Sichuan opera, especially when compared with other genres of Chinese operas. One could even say that the character of the clown is the spiritual embodiment of Sichuan.

> One could even say that the character of the clown is the spiritual embodiment of Sichuan.

In a Sichuan opera play, the clown is not integral to the story being told, but they represent the focal point of the form itself. It is in this character that we see the best representation of the will of an individual on a stage.

> For me, the clown's perspective is the author's perspective.

For me, the clown's perspective is the author's perspective. He is an interlocutory spectre who alone has the power to find a chance of spiritual disengagement amidst moments of comedic relief, to sneak out of the boundaries of the stage to re-examine the story as a narrator and storyteller. The dead protagonist often banters and chants about his life, and though he is immersed in his own folly, he still finds moments of transcendence, as if he were separated from his living self. This is a typical gesture associated with the clown. Thus, the examination of one’s life by one’s dead self became the structure

![Image 2: ree](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/0e9f01_8beb6d846b76412eb5e907de2a667513~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_417,al_c,q_80,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/0e9f01_8beb6d846b76412eb5e907de2a667513~mv2.jpg)

I decided upon. It feels obtuse, but at the same time, it is also sympathetic. The clown jumping in and out between these experiences is a trait especially apparent in Sichuan opera. Maybe the terroir of the Sichuan basin breeds this kind of creative fertility.

In a Sichuan opera play, the clown is also a kind of “magnified” human being. In representations of their humanity, we see contrasting traces of grace/vulgarity, naiveté/cruelty, solemnity/buffoonery, kindness/tenderness, confusion/self-awareness, and fragility/tenacity. Just like the painted face of the clown, it's hard to tell on the outset if this is a joyful or sad character. In this story, all these humble individuals drift with the tidal waves of the changing era. They are powerless to manage their fates against echoing reverberations of desperate situations, but suddenly they find the audacity to guffaw and make a face, however useless, against the tide. This is the glory and defiance of a people who are as minute as a speck of dust. These are people, who after falling into a cesspool, still manage to gracefully separate themselves from the pieces of fecal matter drowning them. The protagonist, as well as everyone else revolving around him in the film, also have this distinct trait. The dust specks dance in the limelight, which ultimately forms an ensemble play of clowns.

_DN: The film tells the story of a Sichuan opera troupe, but you chose to focus on the daily lives of the actors rather than their opera performances. How did you integrate Sichuan opera into this film?_

> I wanted to present a distinctly Sichuan-flavoured saga; a comical epic of the people of Sichuan.

**QJJ:**I wanted to present a distinctly Sichuan-flavoured saga; a comical epic of the people of Sichuan. My main concern lay with the desire to incorporate local elements without making a conceptualized spectacle that reduced these elements to stereotypes. For example, the mask-changing and fire-breathing techniques in Sichuan opera has already mutated into symbolic tourist attractions. I wanted to tell the story in a way that reconstructs the traditional grammar of the Sichuan operatic language which would simulate and retain its flavor and melodies without sacrificing the ability to communicate through a common language, just like the works of Chaucer, Rabelais, Boccaccio, and medieval tramp novels.

Sichuan opera is a timeless heritage with unrestrained and boundless beauty. It is full of mundane expressions that connects us with the deepest and most personal of our humanity. Maybe it's because the land of Sichuan is just so lively, and filled with the hustle and bustle of life, that people residing there are able to cope with their problems as though it’s nothing but daily routine. For example, one often associates Sichuan opera with cuisine. The words "Jiao Ma" (literally "peppery and chili flavor") in the film’s title "Jiao Ma Tang Hui" (the original Chinese title of A NEW OLD PLAY), is literally translated as "the gathering and celebration of peppery and chili flavors.” “Jiao Ma” is a classic Sichuan taste.

In this film, the connection between those onstage and offstage, as well as inside and outside the Sichuan opera being put together in the story, is blurred. What happens onstage is integrated into the narrative, and the expressions onstage are blended into the characters’ everyday lives. This is because Sichuan opera took root in my body and soul through the mundanity of everyday life. Just like when generations of Sichuan opera goers, who spent much of their time in the theater weeping, sighing, falling asleep, etc., their lives are in a way inter-textualized with the performance on stage, creating an adventitious symmetry of life itself; were they just watching a performance, or are they themselves a part of, or even integrated into the performance? With time, the stage actors pass away. The audience passes away. The symmetric organism formed between the performers and the audience disintegrates, and thus Sichuan opera also “passes away". Through the film, I tried to channel the voice of a Sichuan opera clown to conjure the lost bits of these interesting daily lives.

In terms of the form of the film, I tried to express as much as I could through the familiar elements of Chinese operas. For example, on a Chinese opera stage, a table and two chairs can represent a hill and a bridge. A whip can represent a valiant steed. A pair of flags can represent a sedan chair or chariot. Four actors are equivalent to an army consisting of hundreds of thousands of warriors. Chinese operas often find impressionistic, even free-handed ways to paint a world of wonders within a very confined space. I am fascinated with this creativity.

In addition, the music composed for this film was also created from elements taken from traditional Sichuan opera.

_DN: Most of the film’s dialogue (as well as the written screenplay) feature the Sichuan dialect. Why did you choose to use a specific dialect?_

QJJ: I chose to film in the Sichuan dialect because it is my native language. The Sichuan dialect is characterized by its vividness and humor. In 1962, a film titled “Conscription" was filmed in the Sichuan dialect. It’s peculiar in the sense that even though the film was clearly preachy, but the usage of the Sichuan dialect gave it a homely, authentic, and vibrant tone. This film has infludenced generations of Sichuan audiences. Since the early 90s, the Sichuan province has produced many television dramas using our own dialect. In a way, this means that the dialect choice does indeed enjoy an audience base. Unfortunately, however, there has not been another film of note made in the Sichuan dialect since “Conscription”. I suppose this is probably one of the reasons why I chose to use the Sichuan dialect in my film as well. Towards the end of the Ming dynasty, the peasant rebel Zhang Xianzhong committed mass genocide against the Sichuan people. Due to this event, most of the subsequent generations of the Sichuan people are actually migrants from other provinces. Hundreds of years of migration has resulted in the forming of a Sichuan dialect that is complex with tones of vivacity, vulgarity, voracity, and perhaps something indistinguishable between ecstasy and melancholy. It’s a dialect of strong nostalgia that is at once rich and three-dimensional while also wise and transcendent. This is still evident today in my hometown where the mighty and insignificant alike all congregate in the fields of forgotten diaspora, speaking this very same dialect.

> **Hundreds of years of migration has resulted in the forming of a Sichuan dialect that is complex with tones of vivacity, vulgarity, voracity, and perhaps something indistinguishable between ecstasy and melancholy.**

_DN: The film’s depth of field and horizontally-shifting camera work presented a strong, painterly vision. Can you tell us how you came to this stylistic choice?_

QJJ: Painting was the very first artistic endeavor that I took on. Naturally, painting was something that would find a place in my films.

The cinematography in this film, or more specifically, the stylistic choice to emphasize the boundaries of the seen frame, is directly inspired by paintings. For example, the shallow depth of field resembles the narrative style of religious altar triptychs or frescoes of Giotto di Bondone. In terms of camera movement, we used many horizontal shifts to present the story like a slowly unveiling scroll of Chinese painting.

_DN: This film features a very unusual production design style, can you tell us more about how this style came about？_

QJJ: We built a simple white shed on the parking lot of a friend’s factory, and borrowed another manufacturing space within the same factory. These two places, when combined, were roughly about one thousand square meters altogether. That’s all we had to shoot and prepare the sets with.The production design took us about half a year, where we basically hand-made all the elements that are in the film. Pieces from the walls, the staircases, and backdrops all the way down to the most minute items in the film were all hand-crafted and painted by the production design team and myself. During the shooting process, we would disassemble and reassemble the necessary pieces as the scenes required, and planned accordingly. Every time we finished shooting a scene, we might need to disassemble the pieces and reassemble at a later time. The entire shoot took around three months.

> **The production design took us about half a year, where we basically hand-made all the elements that are in the film.**

Many materials were hand-me-downs and just random things laying around that we were able to refurbish through techniques that were passed down from early screen and stage experiences. In a way, I wanted the film to visually convey a sense between reality and fiction. In my previous film, MR. ZHANG BELIEVES, I also used the very same method of sound stage shooting and handcrafting production designs. This film is a continuation of that tradition. I think sound stage shooting and handcrafted production designing is a tradition that is an extension of creative invention. I hope that through connecting myself to said tradition, and translating my own understanding of it in my own film, I can have a spiritual discourse with the history of cinema as a whole.

_DN: Many of the actors in your film are also your crew members. What was the thinking behind this decision？_

QJJ: The people involved in this film are mainly my family. Family, in the broader sense, includes not only my relatives, but also people from my hometown, many of whom have close ties to my relatives. Many of my friends, who I also consider to be my family, not only play roles in the film, but are also involved in the production. In a way, this was a fulfillment of my wish to tell a story locally. The production of this film was a like a party that gathered my family, friends, and co-workers together for a summer bash. A party that connected like-minded people together.

In the film, only the teachers in the troupe are professional Sichuan opera actors. Everyone else are essentially nonprofessional actors. Many of the leads in the film have very deep roots in Chinese independent cinema, whether as directors or producers. For example, the actor who plays Qiu Fu and actress who plays Tong Huafeng (Qiu Fu’s wife), were proliferate curator and coordinator of independent film festivals. The actor who plays Tuo-er is the acclaimed independent documentary director Gu Tao.

From the year 2000 to 2012, Chinese independent films was going through a period of rapid growth. It was during this time that I made many lasting friendships. This film gave us a chance to come back together.

> From the year 2000 to 2012, Chinese independent films was going through a period of rapid growth. It was during this time that I made many lasting friendships. This film gave us a chance to come back together.

Many of my friends in the art circle also joined in the festivities. Artists like Lv Xin, Lu Wei, and Wen Ke were involved since my beginnings in documentary filmmaking. In this film, not only were they leading the production design team, but they also played roles.

My father played Pocky. My nephew played Little Qiu, and my niece played Ah Gui. My cousin composed the music for the film, while my uncle is my artistic advisor. Also of note is that most of our crew all played roles in the film. Just like actors in the Sichuan opera troupes of yore, the crew members would often wear heavy make-up and move set pieces and backdrops in their costumes.

![Image 3: ree](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/0e9f01_ac69ef18a64f4a5988c5d0fa16fe9a4c~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_147,h_83,al_c,q_80,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,blur_2,enc_avif,quality_auto/0e9f01_ac69ef18a64f4a5988c5d0fa16fe9a4c~mv2.jpg)

● 这个电影是取材自你的祖父，是什么促使你做这部电影？

我的祖父是一个川剧小丑名角，从上世纪三四十年代开始就走红四川，直到80年代去世。我人生的最初十年和他相处十分密切，他是我艺术启蒙的关键人物，包括绘画、文学、编导、音乐、表演。在他身上，我第一次认识了幽默、创造力，也形成了对小丑的最初的认识，就是有趣的个体的力量是多么强大。

在这部影片之前我主要做纪录片创作，题材都是身边的亲友的生活史。这些纪录片就像我的绘画一样，都是对肖像生动而细密的刻画，笔法癫狂，色调沉郁，都有小丑的印记。

2017年，在我祖父逝世30周年的时候，我父亲完成了一部关于他的传记，并让我为这本书画了一些插图。在两个月日以继夜的绘制的过程中，我的表达欲和想象力被激发出来，想做一部关于他的剧情电影，一个小丑的故事。父亲的这本传记提供了一些素材，我也做了大量的资料搜集，然后重新用我自己的方式来讲一个经历了时代巨变的普通人一生的故事，充满了小丑的精神。像极了你我他，太阳之下本无新事，我们只是用各自的语法周而复始地传唱。

● 小丑与你而言有何特别之处，你觉得小丑代表了什么？

在中国各种戏剧中，小丑这个行当在川剧中的体现最多。甚至可以说：小丑的性格就是四川的精神。一台本戏中，小丑往往不是故事的关键，却是形式的主体；这是舞台上最能体现个人意志的角色了。

对我来讲，小丑的视角就是作者的视角。他是舞台上的间离天使，灵魂时常会在嬉戏中自如地出窍，偷渡出舞台的边界，作为一个叙述者，一个说书人而存在。死去的主人公对自己的一生进行揶揄和咏唱，时而沉浸，时而超脱，和生时的自己若即若离，这就是典型的小丑姿态。所以我用了这样的结构：就是死者对他一生的审视。它是跳脱的，同时又是切肤的。跳进又跳出的小丑啊，川剧中表现尤甚——可能盆地的风土滋长这种细菌。

小丑也是戏文里某种放大的“人”，人性方面，它结合了优雅、天真、粗鄙、庄严、滑稽、残忍、善良、温柔、浑噩和自觉、脆弱和顽强，就像小丑的面庞，它到底是喜悦还是悲伤？在这个故事里，所有的小人物跟着大时代随波逐流，即便到了绝境，无法改变，但是突然莞尔一笑，做了一个鬼脸，哪怕是无用的，这就是尘埃的光辉。就像掉进粪坑，你还是优雅地把眼前的那坨屎轻轻拨开。在本片中，主角是这样，其他人也都有这样的特质，尘埃们在强光中起舞，他们构成了一出群丑戏。

● 虽然故事中讲述的是一个川剧戏班，但你并没有特别呈现川剧的表演，更多去呈现这些戏班演员的生活，你是如何将川剧融入到这部电影里的？

我想要做一部四川口味的风情长卷，四川人的漫画史诗。我着重考虑的是在地性元素如何不概念化、奇观化、符号化，比如川剧的变脸、吐火。它们已经异化，变成了某种观光与猎奇的项目。我希望一种模仿川剧戏文的方式来表达，其实这是一种人类共同所认知的语法，像坎特伯雷、巨人传、十日谈、中世纪流浪汉小说那样。

川剧高古优美，隽永不羁，而且充满了日常的生活化表达，特别人性化。可能是因为四川这块土地就是烟火气十足，这块土地上的人似乎可以用日常应对一切问题。比如你往往会由川剧联想到食物。《椒麻堂会》的“椒麻”就是典型的一种川菜口味。

川剧在这部影片里，台上台下、戏里戏外的关系是模糊的，舞台上的东西融进了叙事，进行日常化地表现。因为川剧是在日常中进入我的视野和身心的，并且从日常中展开。就像当年川剧的老观众在剧场里消耗他的时间，不管不顾地流泪、唏嘘、睡着了，这一切与舞台上的演出互文，合谋出一块生命场域；他们是在观看还是过日子？后来演员死了，观众死了，日常场域消失，川剧也就“死”了。所以我试图通过影片，用川剧小丑的口吻对这些失传的“有趣的日常”进行一次召唤。

在影片形式上，我尽量用中国戏曲的表达方式去呈现。比如在戏曲舞台上，一张桌子和两把椅子就可以代表山坡、桥梁，一根鞭子就可以代表一匹马，一对旗帜就可以代表车或轿，四个人就可以代表千万大军等等。戏曲总是在有限的空间内，用一种写意的方式去描绘世界。这是让我着迷的方式。

还有，这部影片里的配乐也是用川劇的傳統曲牌作為基本元素而進行的創作。

● 无论是你的剧本写作，还是电影中的对白都是用四川方言完成的，你为什么选择方言？

因为四川方言是我的母语。四川方言的特色就是生动，幽默。1962年有一部四川方言电影——《抓壮丁》——很奇特，明明是在宣讲什么，语调却家常、地道、生机勃勃。这片子影响了好几代的四川观众。九十年代初期以来四川又拍摄了很多方言电视剧，也就是说方言在四川很有群众基础。但遗憾的是，《抓壮丁》以后再没有出现过经典的方言电影。明朝末年的张献忠对四川的本地人进行过大屠杀，现在的川人几乎都是移民的后代。数百年的人口流动形成了四川方言的繁杂、生动、市井、烟火气、土腥味儿十足甚至说不清是狂喜还是忧郁的东西，一种很强烈的乡愁，非常丰富，非常立体，智慧而超然。天地和刍狗，带着口音在田间地头立此存照。

● 这部影片的浅景深以及横移镜头使得影片呈现出强烈的绘画性，可否讲一讲你为什么采取了这样的表达方式？

绘画是我最早从事的艺术工作，绘画性自然会在我的影片里有充分的体现。

在摄影上，對於畫面邊界感的強調直接來自於繪畫的啟示，比如喬托的溼壁畫，淺景深的調度在視覺上像極了在宗教場所的祭壇或神龕裡所展開的敘事。在運鏡上，我們使用了大量的橫移，就像一張中國畫的長卷徐徐展開。

● 这部影片的美术风格不同寻常，请介绍一下你们的制作方式？

我们在一个模具厂的停车场上自己搭了一个简易的白棚，并借用工厂的另一个车间，这两个加起来不到1000平米的地方就是我们所有的置景及拍摄场地。

我们的置景用了小半年的时间，制作场景的基本元素，比如可拆卸的景片、墙体、台阶。电影中的这个世界——所有呈现的元素——都是我们手工创作出来的，所有的墙面和装饰都是我和美术组一笔一画手绘出来的。在拍摄过程中，我们利用这些基本元素进行组装，以场景为单位进行规划，每拍摄完一个场景，就将零件拆卸下来，再次进行组装。整体拍摄历时三个月。

我们运用很多因地制宜、信手拈来的材料以及很多来自早期电影及舞台剧的充满手工感的制作方法，希望使它呈现出虚实相间的效果。我上一部影片《痴》，也是采用了这样棚拍和手工制作的方式。这部影片是它的一个延续。棚拍和手工法属于电影早期的有发明意味的方式，我想通过自己的转译，和电影史进行对话。

● 这部影片的演员往往也同时是你剧组的工作人员，这是一个怎样的团队？

这部影片参与的人主要是我的家人。家人，广义层面来说，不仅包括我的亲人，也有家乡的人，他们多而不少，都会跟我的家族产生关系，还有我的好友。他们不仅是演员，也参与了制作。这也是我在地的书写方式的一种全面实践。

这部电影的制作就像一个聚会，集结了我的家庭、朋友、同僚，就像一个夏日开始的亲友聚会，一场“同类的聚会”。

这部影片除了剧团的老师是专业的川剧演员之外，其余基本都是非职业演员。这部影片的几位主演和中国独立电影都有很深的渊源，或是独立电影的推手，或是导演。比如邱福和他妻子桐花凤的扮演者，就是中国曾经非常活跃的云之南影像展的策展人和组织者。驼儿的扮演者就是中国著名的独立纪录片导演顾桃，鸡脚神的扮演者也是中国一个民间放映组织的创办者。中国独立电影从2000年初到2012年是一个蓬勃发展的时期，我们在这期间结下了深厚的友谊。因为这部影片，我们又聚在了一起。还有我艺术圈的朋友，比如艺术家吕欣、陆苇、温科，他们从我最早的纪录片创作开始就一直参与其中，在这部影片里他们不仅带领了美术部门的工作，也出演了一些角色。参与本片的还有我的亲人，比方我的父亲饰演了pocky，我的侄子饰演了little Qiu，我的侄女饰演了Ah Gui，作曲是我的表妹，我的叔叔既饰演了其中一个角色，同时也是我的艺术顾问之一。值得一提的是，我们的工作人员基本都参与了演出，就像以前川剧班子里的演员，他们身着戏装，画着浓妆，在换场的空隙搬运景片。

1.title: 东注 ARTeFACT - 国际优质视觉内容award-winning creative media company
1.description:
上海东注，由奥斯卡与金马奖得主创立
ARTeFACT Entertainment, founded by Oscars and Taipei Golden Horse Awards winners.
1.content:
Short synopsis

The leading "clown" role in a renowned theatre troupe passes on, and is welcomed into the Underworld. As he relives his vivid memories one last time before entering the afterlife, fifty years of art, struggle and love play out against the background of 20th-century China’s tumultuous history.

Long synopsis

One evening in the 1980s, Qiu Fu, a leading clown-role actor in 20th-century Sichuan opera, departs this world and must reluctantly set off for the Ghost City under the escort of two underworld officials. Along the way, he meets old friends. As they recall the past, earthly scenes creep into the mists of the Netherworld.

Qiu Fu’s life in opera unfolds against the backdrop of a secular upheaval. The "New-New'' Troupe in which he grows up and learns his trade is affiliated with the military. The troupe is cast loose as power shifts to wander rootlessly through a broken world. Despite this unsettled destiny, shaped by war, famine and political turmoil, Qiu Fu becomes one of the finest clown-role performers in Sichuan opera. And yet, one day he finds himself clapped in a pigsty as a political revolution rages outside.

Outside the Ghost City, sitting among familiar faces, Qiu Fu drinks the mandatory bowl of Forgetfulness Soup to erase his memory. A lifetime of hardship, pain and sorrow, all vanish as if they had never been.

_A New Old Play_ — Qiu Jiongjiong
=================================

[May 20, 2022](https://inreviewonline.com/2022/05/20/a-new-old-play-qiu-jiongjiong/)[- by Ryan Swen](https://inreviewonline.com/the-writers/ryan-swen/)

![Image 3: A New Old Play film still. Man smoking, wearing a red cap. Face sculpture on wall. Qiu Jiongjiong film.](https://inreviewonline.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/A-NEW-OLD-PLAY-01_Courtesy-of-the-dGenerate-Collection-at-Icarus-Films-1024x579.jpg)

Credit: the dGenerate Collection at Icarus Films

_A New Old Play_ is a rich, complex contribution to the Chinese folk tradition, and a “theater” film for the ages.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

* * *

Without getting too far into Bresson’s dissection of the irreconcilable differences between the artistic media of film and theater, there has been a longstanding interest, and thus conundrum, in how to depict the staging of a theatrical production on film. From Busby Berkeley backstage musicals to _The Golden Coach_ to Rivette’s masterpieces to _Vanya on 42 nd Street_ to, of course, _Drive My Car_, films about theater are typically just as much about the communal nature of the endeavor, the relationships that are formed in the intimate times of living and working together.

And then, there are those films, like _The Travelling Players_ and _Platform_, that use theater and performance as a means to convey and explore the grand sweep of history, as the relatively static nature of performance and style is met by larger social and governmental forces over decades. Qiu Jiongjiong’s feature debut, _A New Old Play_, fits in very much with this lineage of acting-troupe epics, running just under three hours and spanning the 1920s to the 1980s in the Sichuan Province. Unlike its predecessors, however, it totally focuses on a single actor: a clown, Qiufu, who is based on Qiu’s own grandfather. It also explicitly takes a retrospective look: the film begins with two demons arriving to bring him to hell, and the rest of the film threads this long journey alongside a chronological retelling of his ascent to stardom in the New-New Troupe and Opera School (at age seven), and how he, his family, and his collaborators weathered World War II, the Chinese Civil War, and the upheaval that the Chinese Communist Party introduced into an already fraught environment.

In a sharp break from the documentaries that have made up Qiu’s work to date, _A New Old Play_ instead opts for an approach that emphasizes artificiality and stylization of these spaces of the past and the supernatural. Seemingly every scene takes place on a set, each crafted to maximize what feels like a handcrafted quality to the film, where the distressed and flat personality permeates the backdrops of man-made structures and landscapes alike. A golden statue is embodied by living flesh, ocean currents by billowing fabric, and brick walls look like plywood painstakingly painted to suggest the mortar without fully defining it. All of these might strike one as budgetary necessities, but the effect here is far from, say, the nightmarish distortions of _The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari_ or the opposite approach of reflection of present onto past in _Platform_. Instead, this abstraction suggests an archetypal base to build upon, a physical closeness of space and a continuity between the “real world” and the purposeful unreality of theater, literalized in a shot that tracks right as bricks are rolled on-stage from a daytime view of distant mountains, then off-stage into the painted night sky and distant city. And while Qiu is free to mix up his style, throwing in oblique angles and handheld when necessary, much of the film is shot in single-direction tracking shots and tableaux teeming with people, where the distinctiveness of the faces meld into a tapestry of expressions and reactions, all similar but none totally alike.

That quality serves the film well: Qiufu is certainly the main character, set apart by this supernatural intervention and his obdurate commitment to craft, even as his fellow cast and crew fall away due to the ravages of time, while also being instantly recognizable thanks to his ever-present large ears, red nose, and beanie. But this is as much a portrait of community, leaving plenty of time to consider how people contend with the weight of change and history, each interaction another building block in a conception of history that is resolutely intimate and aggregative. Even the intertitles that help clarify when the next decade has passed for those very unfamiliar with Chinese history — as someone of Chinese descent, the careful but never overstated intertwining of history into the narrative moved me — convey these changes in more poetic terms.

All this while, Qiufu is on his way to the afterlife, where he will have to drink a soup of forgetfulness to enter, or otherwise wander as a ghost among the living. This voyage into the unknown carries the same genial tone as _A New Old Play_, of a resigned acceptance of the inevitable that carries with it a whole world of mystery and discovery. The film closes with Qiu himself appearing in front of the camera, one of the most fitting cameos in ages, as he implicitly puts himself in the lineage of these performers and artists who have contributed to a rich Chinese folk tradition. On the strength of _A New Old Play_, such a gesture is more than earned.

Qiu Jiongjiong and _A New Old Play_
===================================

By [David Hudson](https://www.criterion.com/current/author/654-david-hudson)

[The Daily](https://www.criterion.com/current/category/20-the-daily)—

Share

![Image 2: A group of young people and one adult in vintage clothing stand in front of a brick wall with a painted background](https://criterion-production.s3.amazonaws.com/TUobxGnRBoSlZrc5qAbjfa5HDRAN7v.jpg)

 Qiu Jiongjiong’s _A New Old Play_ (2021) 

C hinese artist and filmmaker Qiu Jiongjiong was only two when he began [painting](http://www.stargallery.cn/en/artists/detail/58) and three when he first performed Sichuan opera. In the mid-1990s, he left school at the age of eighteen to pursue his art, and in 2006, he bought a mini-DV camera and began shooting documentaries. When [_A New Old Play,_](https://icarusfilms.com/df-newold) his first fictional feature, premiered in Locarno last summer, it won a Special Jury Prize, and before the film begins its tour of North American theaters at [Anthology Film Archives](http://anthologyfilmarchives.org/film_screenings/calendar?view=list&month=05&year=2022#showing-54526) on May 20, the National Museum of Asian Art will present an online retrospective. [The Daring, Innovative Films of Qiu Jiongjiong](https://asia.si.edu/events-overview/films/?trumbaEmbed=view%3Dseries%26seriesid%3D1643856) will be freely accessible from this Friday through May 29.

“Without formal cinematic training, Qiu started as a fearless eccentric, creating experimental documentaries with the series of effervescent, slyly humorous family portraits,” writes [Shelly Kraicer](https://asia.si.edu/an-introduction-to-qiu-jiongjiong/) in the introduction to the program he first put together for [Rotterdam](https://iffr.com/en/expanded/2022/focus-qiu-jiongjiong) earlier this year. Qiu “cuts rapidly but always legibly between different materials and times in his six documentaries, with a darting, cheerfully voyeuristic handheld camera that captures striking black-and-white images. Sound and image are often provocatively decoupled; Qiu underlays these elements with traditional Sichuan opera and contemporary art music.”

In 2016, [Kang Kang](https://brooklynrail.org/2016/05/film/qiu-jiongjiong-with-kang-kang) spoke with Qiu for the _Brooklyn Rail_ about _Mr. Zhang Believes_ (2015), which blends fiction and nonfiction to tell the story of Zhang Xianchi, a young communist who turned his back on his nationalist father to join the People’s Liberation Army—but was nonetheless tossed behind bars for more than two decades during the Anti-Rightist Movement of the 1950s. “Shot in color and de-saturated into a surreal black-and-white,” writes Kang in the introduction to his interview, “Zhang’s first-person account of the revolution devouring its own children is transformed by Qiu’s highly stylized set and sound design, Brechtian amateur acting, and contrapuntal editing into a dizzying shadow play of figures and objects—herein lies a profane illumination of sorts, coinciding with the elderly Zhang’s eventual coming into consciousness.”

One of Qiu’s earliest documentaries, _Ode to Joy_ (2008) is a tribute to his grandfather, Qiu Fuxin, a renowned comedic performer with the Xinyouxin Opera Troupe. Qiu drew inspiration from his grandfather again to create Qiu Yu, the Sichuan opera “clown” at the center of _A New Old Play._ As the old man dies, his departing soul revisits his memories, “starting,” notes [Daniel Kasman](https://mubi.com/notebook/posts/state-of-the-festival-locarno-2021) in the Notebook, “with the troupes’ creation during the chaotic period of the 1920s before passing through war with Japan, the nationalists’ struggles, war with the ascendant communists, a trip to Taiwan, and a gradual dissolution of the players before Mao’s secured reign . . . Qiu has made a cleverly contained existential epic, an ode to the innate persistence of workers, artists, and people in the face of futility and poor fortune. It is a wonder the film carries it off with an empathetic sparkle.”
